The user wants a short explanation of why caching improves web performance. I need to cover what a cache is, where caches live, and the tradeoffs.

A cache stores copies of responses closer to where they are needed. Browsers keep a local cache, CDNs keep edge caches near users, and servers can cache computed results in memory.

The main benefit is avoiding repeated work and network round trips. A cached asset can be served in milliseconds instead of hundreds of milliseconds across the internet.

The tradeoff is staleness. If the underlying data changes, cached copies may serve outdated content, so headers like Cache-Control and validation with ETags matter.

Let me think about how to structure this. Maybe start with the definition, then the layers, then the staleness tradeoff, and end with a practical tip about cache headers.

I should also mention that caching reduces load on the origin server, which helps under traffic spikes. That is often as important as latency for real systems.

I think the structure is fine. Definition, layers, benefits for latency and load, then staleness and how headers control it. That covers the question well without going too deep.

One more consideration: private versus shared caches. Personalized responses should not be stored in shared caches, which is what the private directive is for. I will add a sentence on that.

Alright, the outline is complete and covers definition, layers, benefits, staleness, and the private directive.
